title: Remarks at Bridgeport, Connecticut
paragraphs: Mr. Mayor, and you my fellow citizens, my fellow Americans:

I shall detain you but one moment. There was an accident to the party to-day, to the carriage I was in, which resulted in the death of one of the men and another is seriously, perhaps fatally injured. The man who was killed was one whom I was very fond of and whom I highly prized for his loyalty and his faithfulness, and under these circumstances I am sure you will not mind my not making you a formal address, but simply expressing to all of you my gratitude and appreciation for the wonderful reception that you have given, not me, but the President of the United States. (Applause) I thank you all with all my heart. I thank the men of the Grand Army, the men who proved true to a lofty ideal when the days called not merely for work but for risking everything, life itself on the alta [?]r of the country. I thank my younger comrades of the Spanish American War, and above all I wish to express my profound appreciation of the guard of honor, and I say that I can not imagine [?] any American President having a more appropriate guard of honor than such a one as I had to-day, representing chiefly the wage-workers of this industrial town. I not only wish to thank them for the courtesy that they showed me in thus turning out as my guard of honor, but I congratulate them upon the extreme efficiency with which they did their work. It would be impossible to have a better managed and better handled parade than this has been, and it has been thus handled because of the extreme efficiency with which the guard of honor throughout the more than seven miles kept the road absolutely clear. I thank you all, gentlemen. I thank those of the national guard. I appreciate very deeply what it has meant thus to be received by you, men and women, my friends and neighbors, my fellow countrymen, in this way. I am deeply obliged to you. I know you will not regard me as churlish because under the circumstances I do not make a formal address to you; and because of those circumstances I shall ask further, if you are willing, that you do not applaud or make any manifestation of saying goodbye to me. The friend who was killed beside [?] me is now lying unburied. I shall close by simply again expressing to you my profound gratitude and appreciation of your greeting.

The last six lines ("I know you will not regard me ... appreciation") are typed single-spaced in a block, apparently added after the rest. Hand corrections: commas after "to-day", "in", "all", "you" (men and women) and "further"; "not", "And", "of" (replaced by "in"), "by" and "and" struck through in ink; "more than" written above a struck word (probably "over"); "of your greeting." written at the end. In "altar" and "imagine" the vowel is blotted or overwritten and the reading is not certain; "friend" has an overwritten r. The right half of frame 0642 (folio 171) carries only a handwritten note: "The following Addresses are corrected copies of Prepared Speeches, giving them as they were delivered by the President." Third look: the ink stroke through "by" runs up past (not through) "me" to a hand word in the right margin that replaces "by"; it reads "besi..." and runs off the edge of the sheet, so "beside" is uncertain. After "imagine" the ink is a hand-written "e" over the typed letter with a rising exit stroke, not a comma (hand commas on this page are short vertical strokes), so no comma is recorded.
